hero.subtitle_html: Linthal → Fridolinshütte — SAC T4 · ~1460 m gain · ~8 km one-way · overnight option

intro_html:
"Tödi is the highest point in the canton of Glarus — a massive glacier mountain that guards the head of the Linth valley. The approach to the Fridolinshütte is one of the great valley walks of the Glarus Alps: remote, dramatic, and increasingly wild as the glacier comes into view."

This hike goes to the Fridolinshütte SAC hut (2111 m), the classic base camp for summit attempts on Tödi. The route from Linthal through the Limmerental valley is graded T4 — sure-footedness and alpine experience are required, but no glacier equipment. The final push to the summit (3614 m) requires crampons, ice axe, and rope; that section is rated T5+/PD and is not part of this hike. The hut itself — with its stunning glacier panorama — is a magnificent destination in its own right, either as a long day hike or an overnight before a summit bid.
quick_facts: Tödi, 3614 m (highest point in Glarus canton)
T4 — alpine hiking, sure-footedness essential
~4–5 h ascent · ~3 h descent · 7–8 h total
Fridolinshütte — sleeps ~90, staffed June–September; advance booking strongly recommended
T5+/PD from the hut — glacier equipment (crampons, ice axe, rope) required; NOT covered here
Late June to mid-October (hut staffed); snow may persist longer

bullets_html: Start at Linthal train station (~650 m). Follow the valley road / trail into the Limmerental.
The path ascends steadily through the Limmerental — a long, progressively remote alpine valley.
Pass Tierfed (~1100 m), where the terrain becomes more demanding and trail conditions more variable.
Upper section involves rocky path, route-finding on alpine terrain, and some exposed passages — characteristic T4 ground.
Arrive at Fridolinshütte SAC hut (2111 m) — spectacular glacier panorama of Tödi and Bifertenstock.
Ascent: ~1460 m gain, ~8 km, 4–5 h. Descent: ~3 h. Total round-trip ~7–8 h.
Overnight option: book the hut, rest, then ascend to the summit (T5+/PD, glacier equipment required) the next morning.

routes.title_html: 2. Summit ascent: Fridolinshütte → Tödi summit (3614 m) — T5+/PD
bullets_html: NOT covered by this hike page. The summit requires alpine mountaineering skills.
From the hut, cross the glacier (crampons + ice axe + rope mandatory). Crevasse hazard — guided or very experienced parties only.
Typically undertaken as an early-morning start from the hut (alpine start ~3–5 am).
This extension is rated PD in the UIAA/SAC alpine scale — not a hiking grade.

getting_there.by_pt_html:
• Train: Zürich HB → Linthal (~1.5 h). Typical route: Zürich HB → Ziegelbrücke → Schwanden → Linthal (change at Ziegelbrücke or Schwanden; check sbb.ch).
  • Alternatively: Zürich HB → Glarus → Linthal (S-Bahn to Glarus then Glarner regional train).
  • Linthal is the terminus of the Glarner regional railway — frequent trains from Schwanden and Glarus.
  • Return trains from Linthal run into the evening — check SBB for last departure.
getting_there.by_car_html: Drive to Linthal via the A3 motorway → Glarus → cantonal road through the Linth valley. Parking available at Linthal train station. The road beyond Linthal into the Limmerental may have seasonal restrictions — confirm locally. Some visitors drive further to Tierfed (limited parking) to shorten the approach by ~4 km each way.

day_plans.title: Day Hike (T4 — Linthal → Fridolinshütte and back)
rows: Start hiking from Linthal station (~650 m)
Tierfed (~1100 m) — terrain becomes more alpine
Fridolinshütte (2111 m) — lunch, glacier views, ~4.5 h ascent
day_plans.footer_html: Start early — afternoon thunderstorms are common in the Glarus Alps. The upper valley is exposed. Allow extra time on T4 terrain if not accustomed to alpine hiking.

day_plans.title: Overnight Option (hut night + optional summit)
rows: Arrive Fridolinshütte — check in, rest, dinner
Alpine start for summit (glacier team only, PD-rated)
Tödi summit (3614 m) — or return to hut if summit skipped
day_plans.footer_html: Hut booking: Fridolinshütte SAC hut — sleeps ~90, staffed June–September. Book well in advance, especially for weekends in July–August. Summit attempt requires glacier equipment and experience — go with a guide if in doubt.

lapse_rate.example_html: Example: valley forecast 18 °C at Linthal → hut (2111 m) ≈ 9 °C. The glacier and summit (3614 m) will be near or below freezing in most conditions.

sources_html: MeteoSwiss — definitive Swiss forecast. Use the Linthal or Glarus point forecast and check the regional mountain weather bulletin.
Meteoblue Linthal — hourly forecast with cloud-base and precipitation.
Bergfex Glarus — mountain weather and local trail condition reports.
Thunderstorms build rapidly over the Glarus Alps — if afternoon convection is forecast, be at the hut or descending by 13:00.
weather.season_html: Summer hike only. Fridolinshütte is staffed June–September. Outside this window the hut is unstaffed (emergency shelter only), and significant snow may cover the upper trail. Do not attempt without hut confirmation and current snow conditions.

webcams.label: Hoher Kasten (1794 m, Appenzell) — panoramic view looking south across the Glarus Alps; excellent cloud-level indicator for the Tödi area.
Wildhaus / Gamserrugg (Toggenburg, ~1100 m) — looking south-west toward the Glarus Alps; useful for gauging approach visibility.

takeaways_html: The first part of the route from Linthal through the lower Limmerental is straightforward valley hiking — but the trail becomes increasingly demanding as you approach the upper cirque and the Fridolinshütte. Budget 4–5 h for the ascent and do not underestimate the upper T4 section.

The Fridolinshütte is a genuine alpine hut, not a restaurant — book well in advance (especially July/August weekends) and check staffing dates on the SAC website. Arriving without a booking on a busy summer weekend is a gamble.

Glacier approach from the hut (for those attempting the summit) requires a very early alpine start (~3–4 am), a rope team, crampons, and ice axe. Crevasse danger on the Bifertenfirn glacier is real — unroped travel is not appropriate.
The Limmerental valley offers one of the most dramatic enclosed glacier panoramas in the northern Swiss Alps — the hike to the hut is fully rewarding even without any summit ambition.

reports.title: Fridolinshütte — Glacier Views Without the Summit
bullets_html: Day hike from Linthal: 4.5 h to the hut on solid T4 terrain — rocky upper section with occasional cairns.
Fridolinshütte in perfect condition, warm welcome from the guardian; lunch with direct views onto the Tödi glacier.
Descent in ~2.5 h — knees felt it on the lower valley track. Trekking poles strongly recommended.

reports.title: Tödi Überschreitung — Fridolinshütte Overnight + Summit
bullets_html: Classic two-day format: arrive Fridolinshütte mid-afternoon Day 1, alpine start at 4 am Day 2.
Glacier crossing required equipment: crampons, ice axe, 30 m rope — no exceptions, seracs visible from the hut.
Summit conditions excellent in late July; descent via the same route back to Linthal completed by 3 pm Day 2.

reports.title: Limmerental: Linthal bis Fridolinshütte — Herbststimmung
bullets_html: October ascent: first snow on the upper section above ~1800 m — microspikes useful for the final 300 m to the hut.
Hut still open (first weekend of October), but already quiet — only a small group of mountaineers.
The valley in autumn light is extraordinary — larch yellow against grey granite and white glacier.

gear.title: Mandatory (T4 hike to Fridolinshütte)
items_html: Stiff hiking boots with ankle support (B/C category)
Trekking poles — essential on the steep descent
3 L water minimum (no reliable refill on upper route)
High-energy food + emergency snack
Sun protection: hat, sunglasses, SPF 50+ (glacier reflection even from the hut)
Insulating layer + windproof/waterproof shell (2111 m can be cold and windy even in summer)
Hat and gloves (temperatures near the hut routinely drop below 10 °C)
Headlamp (hut overnight, or if descent runs late)
Phone with offline SwissTopo map + downloaded GPX
Small first-aid kit
Hut reservation confirmation

gear.title: Recommended
items_html: Microspikes (late spring / early autumn — snow on upper section likely)
Power bank
Camera with telephoto — glacier and summit details are spectacular from the hut
Gaiters (wet trail in the valley section after rain)

gear.title: Summit attempt only (NOT for the T4 hike)
items_html: Crampons (12-point, compatible with stiff mountaineering boots)
Ice axe
Rope (30–40 m per team)
Harness + glacier travel hardware
Crevasse rescue equipment
Guide or very experienced alpine partner

safety_html: T4 terrain: the upper section of the Limmerental involves rocky, loose, and potentially wet terrain. A slip can be serious — focus and sure-footedness required.

Glacier hazard above the hut: the Tödi glacier (Bifertenfirn) is immediately above the hut. Do not venture onto the glacier without crampons, ice axe, rope, and glacier travel experience — crevasses are present.
Afternoon thunderstorms: the Glarus Alps see frequent convective storms in summer. Be at the hut or well into descent by 13:00–14:00 if instability is forecast.
Snow: the upper trail may carry significant snow from late spring through June, and from October. Check current conditions with the hut guardian before setting out.
Hut reservation: the Fridolinshütte fills quickly on summer weekends. Do not arrive without a booking. The hut guardian can be reached via the SAC hut portal.
Remote terrain: the upper Limmerental has limited phone reception. Download offline maps (SwissTopo / Swisstopo app) and carry the GPX track.
This is a summer-only route. Winter ascent involves serious avalanche terrain — the valley is avalanche-prone in winter and spring.

disclaimer_html: Compiled from SAC route documentation, German Wikipedia, hikr.org community reports, and general alpine knowledge. Not professional mountain-safety or guiding advice. The Tödi approach involves genuine T4 alpine terrain; the summit is a serious glacier mountaineering objective (PD). Conditions in the Glarus Alps change rapidly — always re-check MeteoSwiss, hut guardian advice, and current snow/glacier reports before setting out. If in doubt about your fitness for T4 terrain, or about glacier travel for a summit attempt, hire a certified UIAGM guide.
